notes.claim: Dan's course flowchart is headed "Electrical Circuit Design Calculation Process" for BS 7671:2018 + Amd2:2022, and its note 2 separates a suitable protective conductor size from the minimum protective conductor size.
The showroom supply is three phase four wire 400 V, TN-C-S, with Ze declared as 0.1 ohm and a prospective fault current of 4.6 kA; the ambient temperature is 20 degrees Celsius.
The showroom adds a 400 V three-phase 11 kW motor at power factor 0.8 lagging and efficiency 86%, controlled by a star-delta starter.
Overload protection is the condition Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz (Regulation 433.1.1), plus I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz, where I2 is the current causing effective operation of the protective device.
The course slides take √3 as 1.73, so their printed answers can differ in the last decimal places from the same sum worked with the calculator's √3.
Design current is the magnitude of the current to be carried by a circuit in normal service; the course slides and an IET article give the same meaning.
For a three-phase load with known power factor and efficiency, Ib = P / (VL × Eff × PF × √3), where P is the output of the load and VL is the line-to-line voltage (400 V).
Motors need more current than expected for their output because of reactance, so power factor matters: a lower power factor means more apparent power, and so more current, for the same real power.

Efficiency is useful output power divided by input power, so the supply must provide more than the output; the slides show an efficiency and power factor left out would size the cable on 28.86 A rather than 41.47 A.
Three-phase real power is √3 × line voltage × line current × power factor, which is why Ib divides by √3 × VL × Eff × PF.
If a separate voltage is given, for example at a sub-board, that value is used in place of 230 V or 400 V; the slides work 20 kW at 393 V as 29.38 A.

In a balanced delta load the line current is the phase (winding) current times the square root of 3, so each winding carries the line current divided by √3; in star the line and phase currents are equal.
Diversity percentages are only found in the On-Site Guide and are guidance that need not be applied; the slides' example designs ten 100 W lamps at 66%, or 660 W, rather than 1000 W.
For i1 (review fix): the slides' 66% diversity example is for a domestic lighting circuit, from the On-Site Guide's Appendix A.

For i1 (review fix): at a reduced voltage a resistive heater draws proportionally less current, while a motor draws more to keep its torque, so the slides' same-power working at a sub-board's voltage errs on the safe side for a heater.

For i1 (review fix): the showroom's motor is controlled by a star-delta starter, which runs six wires to the motor, one to each end of each winding, so in delta each of those cables carries one winding's current.
BS 7671 itself has no diversity table; Regulation 311.1 asks the designer to assess maximum demand (of the whole installation or a part of it), and the On-Site Guide gives the recognised figures.
Maximum demand is the largest current an installation draws at any one time, which is why the supply and every submain are sized from it.
Diversity is common-sense guidance from the On-Site Guide's Appendix A, not a rule; the slides give 66% for a domestic lighting circuit as the example.

Sources differ on where diversity is applied: the course slides apply 66% to the Ib of a lighting circuit, while a training provider says diversity applies to the aggregate demand at the origin, not to individual circuits.
notes.contested: Dan's slides apply diversity to the design current of a lighting circuit; Total Skills says to size each circuit on its full design current and apply diversity only to the aggregate demand.

notes.claim: The assignment asks for loads to be balanced across circuits (question 1b), links this to the maximum-demand question 10, and points to Section 3 of The Electrical Installation Guide for demand and diversity factors.
Balanced fundamental currents leave no current in the neutral (a balanced motor load needs no neutral), and an IET forum contributor suggests spreading demand about one third to each phase.
For the EV charge points the guide says load management may be considered to reduce maximum demand but is not compulsory, and Regulation 722.311 lets load curtailment be taken into account.

The lighting drawing's key gives each fitting's wattage (for example 4 × 36 W modular fluorescent, 58 W twin fluorescent, 70 W column luminaires), to be recounted by hand; the power drawing marks 63 A isolators and 2 × 32 A EV points.

Dan's Level 4 specification asks him to state the purpose of diversity factors and to determine the maximum demand of an installation after diversity, covering the application of the IET On-Site Guide.
The slides give the purpose of diversity as designing with 'common sense' rather than the maximum demand, which keeps cable sizes smaller and costs lower (the points for the Section B answer).

For small shops, stores, offices and business premises the On-Site Guide's diversity table gives: lighting 90% of total current demand; heating and power 100% of the largest appliance plus 75% of the remaining appliances; motors (not lifts) 100% of the largest motor plus 80% of the second and 60% of the rest; socket-outlets 100% of the largest point plus 70% of every other point; standard final-circuit arrangements 100% of the largest circuit plus 50% of every other. A showroom is taken to fit this column, which is the course's own assumption.

Sources differ on the small-shop socket-outlet allowance: the table as printed by an electrician's page gives 70% of every other point, an older book (16th Edition era) gives 75%, and the table is numbered A2, H2 or 1B depending on the source and edition, so the lesson names the rule and sends him to his own copy for the figure.
notes.contested: One page prints 100% of the largest point plus 70% of every other point for small shops; an older book prints 100%X + 75%(Y+Z). Table numbering also differs between sources.

notes.claim: For electric vehicle charging: the original 2018 text allowed no diversity on a final circuit with more than one charging point and diversity on a dedicated distribution circuit only with load control; Amendment 1 replaced that with Regulation 722.311.201, which lets load curtailment be taken into account; the IEC wording sets the diversity factor at 1 unless a load management system is used, and the Schneider guide takes the utilisation factor as 1.

Whether Amendment 1 allows any diversity on EV charging is argued on the IET forum: one contributor says BS 7671 does not prohibit it, another that without load management it is still zero diversity; the lesson takes none without load management.
notes.contested: gkenyon (IET EngX): BS 7671 does not prohibit diversity for EV charging points. pww235: in the absence of a load management system it is still zero diversity.

notes.claim: Where diversity is applied is argued: the On-Site Guide table is applied by type of final circuit; the Schneider guide applies its simultaneity factor to a group of loads fed from a distribution board and says the designer is responsible for it; an IET webinar answer says for a single circuit's design current diversity might only rarely be appropriate; an older book says distribution boards must carry their total connected load; the Schneider guide also advises simultaneity factors close to unity when the circuits are mainly lighting.
notes.contested: Sources disagree on whether diversity belongs on each circuit's design current (the slides' 66% example), on a group of circuits at a board, or only on the aggregate at the origin.

notes.claim: Maximum demand is the largest current normally carried by circuits, switches and protective devices; the IET describes it as the sum of the connected loads multiplied by a factor for diversity, and accepts that with diversity applied it may occasionally be exceeded; a forum contributor says the 'official' maximum demand is the rating of the supply fuse.
notes.contested: IET webinar: maximum demand is the connected load multiplied by a diversity factor. An IET EngX contributor: the official maximum demand is the supply fuse rating. The lesson uses the designer's assessment (Regulation 311.1) and says so.

notes.claim: A page on diversity warns that the On-Site Guide's table is aimed at small domestic and similar installations and that commercial and industrial maximum demand may need load measurements or building-services standards, so a showroom with an 11 kW motor and EV points rests on informed assumptions, as question 10 asks.

For a lighting load from a key wattage: the tube power marked on a fluorescent lamp excludes the ballast, 25% of Pn may be used when no ballast loss is given, and cos φ is 0.96 with an electronic ballast; an older book gives current = lamp power x 1.8 / voltage for discharge lighting when the power factor is not below 0.85; each lampholder counts at least 100 W; a separated LED driver's power is not in the module's marked watts, and makers' datasheets for 36 W LED panels state power factors of 0.97 and 0.95.

To balance a three-phase board, single-phase circuits are spread about equally over L1, L2 and L3 because unbalanced line currents do not cancel in the neutral; the most heavily loaded phase fixes the supply requirement; and with a perfect balance the three-phase line current is the total single-phase current divided by three, as an older book works it. Dan's guide asks for a schedule of circuits and his slides say a balanced three-phase load carries no neutral current.

The motor is the only motor on the case, so in the small-shop column it counts at 100% of its full-load current (23.08 A); the Schneider guide instead applies a utilisation factor of about 0.75 to motors in an industrial installation, a different method that the lesson names but does not use.
notes.contested: On-Site Guide small-shop column: 100% of the largest motor. Schneider guide: utilisation factor ku about 0.75 for motors in industrial installations, plus a separate simultaneity factor.

notes.claim: The power drawing's key marks twin switched sockets, 20 A DP switches, a 32 A rotary isolator, 63 A TPN isolators and EV points of 2 x 32 A each, with each charging point having two outlets; the equipment behind the 20 A and 32 A switches is not stated, so the loads there are practice values.

The lighting drawing's key adds a 26 W LED fitting, a wall spot light of 2 x 35 W, an 18 W walkway bollard and an 18 W IP65 bulkhead to the fluorescent and column fittings already noted; the lamp types behind the spot and column fittings are not stated.
Regulation 433.1.1 requires In not less than Ib, In not above the lowest Iz of the circuit conductors, and I2 not above 1.45 Iz; the slides write the first two as Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz.

Anything that makes the cable artificially warm, such as thermal insulation or a higher ambient temperature, needs a rating factor; Ca is for ambient temperature, Cg for grouping and Ci for thermal insulation.

Rating factors are applied as divisors to In, giving the tabulated current It the cable needs; It is the tabulated figure for a single circuit at the table's ambient, while Iz is the capacity as installed.
Only factors that act together are combined; the slides' 3 kW heater gives It = 21.2 A (Ca and Cg) and 19.3 A (Ca and Ci) and designs to the higher, on the reference method with the lowest Iz.
A device's I2 is typically 1.45 times In (a 10 A type B breaker: 14.5 A), and the cable must withstand it: for Iz = 13 A the check is I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz, that is 14.5 against 18.85 A.
A semi-enclosed (rewireable) BS 3036 fuse has an I2 that can be up to 2 × Iz, so its In must not exceed 0.725 × Iz, which the slides put in as Cf = 0.725.

Circuit-breaker types B, C and D relate to the start-up current of the circuit; the assignment asks for cables from the starter to the motor to be chosen on delta running conditions and other factors present.

Table 4B1 in his copy of BS 7671 has no 20 °C row: it starts at 25 °C, where the factor for 90 °C thermosetting cable is 1.02 (1.00 at 30 °C). Below 30 °C the factor is above 1; a 20 °C ambient has no value in the book, so the lesson uses a labelled practice value (1.00, which takes no credit for the cool room).
Appendix 4 of BS 7671 is informative, and other methods (for example a cable maker's own data) are legitimate, so the tables are taught as the usual way to show compliance, not the only one.

Six single-core conductors from a star-delta starter all carry the winding current in delta running; Table 4C1 treats n single-core cables as n/3 circuits of three loaded conductors, so six singles are two three-phase circuits, and bunched and enclosed, two circuits give Cg = 0.80.

A thermal overload relay in the delta circuit of a star-delta starter is set to 0.58 times the motor In (the winding current) and must not be set higher than it, so the starter-to-motor cables are sized on 23.08 A ÷ √3 = 13.33 A, not on the line current (a relay in the incoming line, as in the Schneider type 2 coordination, is set to the full motor In instead).

Table 4E1A (90 °C thermosetting singles, copper), Reference Method B, the column for 3 or 4 loaded cables on three-phase AC, gives 15 A for 1 mm² and 20 A for 1.5 mm²; Reference Method B is conduit on a wall or in trunking, and the IET adds that a conduit fixed to a masonry wall may carry more than the tabulated value.

Circuit-breaker type follows the starting current: type B trips instantaneously at 3 to 5 In, type C at 5 to 10 In (suited to small motors and fluorescent-lighting surges) and type D at 10 to 20 In (high inrush); a motor takes a much higher current starting than running, so a device must be chosen not to trip on it, and the standard breaker ratings include 25 A.

A star-delta start draws roughly 2 to 2.7 times full-load current against 6 to 8 times for direct-on-line (a calculator site's table, not a standard); the motor's nameplate or maker gives the true figure, so the lesson uses it only as a labelled practice value.

A breaker to BS EN 60898 has a conventional tripping current of 1.45 In within 1 hour (up to 63 A), so I2 = 1.45 In; a thermal overload relay is not one of those devices, so its own characteristic must be checked against Iz; the slides (p.30) say it takes 10,000 s, which is where Appendix 3's curves end rather than the conventional time. For breakers and gG fuses, Regulation 433.1.201 says that meeting Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz also meets I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz.

Lightly loaded cables leave the group: a cable expected to carry no more than 30 % of its grouped rating may be ignored when finding the group factor for the rest of the group (Table 4C1 note 9), the point of C&G practice paper 1 question 10b.

A hazard of overload is overheating of the circuit conductors, which over time damages insulation, joints and terminations and their surroundings and can lead to fire; BS 7671 also expects a circuit to be designed so that a small overload of long duration is unlikely.

His project guide points to "section 4.7 of The Electrical Installation Guide" for the motor question; which book that is could not be established, so the lesson cites the starter makers and Table 4C1 instead.

For i3 (review fixes): the maker's catalogue gives type B breakers to IEC/EN 60898-1 from 6 to 63 A operation within 1 hour at 1.45 In, while the slides (p.30) say a device at I2 can take 10,000 s: the sources differ on the time. Table 4E1A note 1 (his copy p.458) rates 90 °C cables at the lower temperature of the equipment they connect to; at 70 °C, Table 4D1A column 5 (his copy p.448) gives 1.5 mm² 15.5 A.
Third and other triple harmonic currents of a three-phase load are additive in the neutral and give additional heating of the cables, while the fundamentals of a balanced load cancel there.
Loads such as rectifiers, variable-speed drives and fluorescent lighting banks draw non-sinusoidal currents, so current can appear in the neutral where a balanced motor load would have none.

The neutral current can reach about 173% of phase current in a balanced system with these pulses, and one paper puts triplen neutral current at up to 3 times the phase fundamental, depending on how the percentage is referred.
The slides take the neutral current as Ibn = 3 × h × IL (3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.5 A at 35%), which exceeds the 150 A line current, so Ibn becomes Ib.
The Table 4Aa bands in the slides: line current governs with factor 0.86 for 15 to 33% third harmonic, and above 33% the factor is applied to a calculated neutral current, not the line current.
Harmonics are only considered when the manufacturer's data says one is present; with no neutral conductor there can be no current in it.
The slides' worked example uses It ≥ 160 / (0.94 × 0.65 × 0.86) with the harmonic rating factor included in the divisor.

Table 4Aa, as the slides give it, has four bands by the third harmonic of the line current: 0 to 15% line current with factor 1.0, 15 to 33% line current with 0.86, 33 to 45% neutral current with 0.86, and over 45% neutral current with 1.0; the same table appears in IEC 60364-5-52 (E.52.1) as set out in the Schneider guide, and an IET forum answer ties it to Appendix 4 of BS 7671:2018+A2:2022.

The neutral current is 3 × h × IL: the third and other triple harmonics of the three lines add in the neutral to a magnitude equal to the sum of the third harmonic content of each phase, which is why the slides call the neutral higher than the line at 35% (row 3) and take Ibn as Ib.

Above 33% the neutral current is the larger, so the cable is sized on it; at 45% it is 135% of the line current and the three line conductors are then not fully loaded, which is why the factor goes back to 1.0 above 45%; the Schneider guide works 40% (37 × 0.4 × 3 = 44.4 A, ÷ 0.86 = 51.6 A) as an example.

The ordinary current tables assume three loaded conductors; a harmonic neutral makes a fourth, and BS 7671 treats a neutral as a loaded conductor where a third harmonic or its multiples present a distortion above 15% of the line current (523.6.1) or where it carries current without a matching fall in the line conductors (523.6.3). NICEIC words the 15% as total harmonic distortion where the slides say the third harmonic.
notes.contested: The slides and Table 4Aa speak of the third harmonic content of the line current; NICEIC's summary of Regulation 523.6.1 speaks of total harmonic distortion greater than 15% of the fundamental. Makers usually print a THD figure, so the figure the lesson uses is a practice value for the third harmonic, said so.

notes.claim: Where the neutral current comes only from an imbalance in the line currents, the neutral's heat is offset by less heat in a line conductor, so the cable is sized on the highest line current (NICEIC on 523.6.2); harmonic current is the case where there is no such offset.

The slides' worked example runs from the neutral current to the cable: Ibn 157.5 A is Ib, In 160 A from Fig 3A3(b), It = 160 ÷ (0.94 × 0.65 × 0.86), and Table 4D1A column 5 gives 240 mm² at 346 A (his copy of the table, p.448, row 240: Reference Method B, three or four loaded cables, 346 A).

Harmonics are considered only when the maker's data says there are some, and then the maker's percentage goes into the same sums; makers print THD, not the third harmonic alone: a Thorn luminaire datasheet gives THD 15.00 %, and a Philips Advance (US, 60 Hz) ballast table gives fluorescent ballasts as less than 25% THD (conventional magnetic), less than 20% (standard electronic) and less than 10% (Centium electronic).

No limit is quoted here for a fluorescent fitting's third harmonic in the showroom's drawing: the ANSI standard for electronic ballasts allows a maximum THD of 32%; IEC 61000-3-2 Class C (lighting, input current up to 16 A per phase) limits the third harmonic to 30 × the circuit power factor in percent; the absolute harmonic current matters more than the percentage; and the On-Site Guide says discharge-lighting final circuits must carry the lamps' and controlgear's harmonic currents (its ×1.8 volt-ampere rule includes harmonic current).
Voltage drop is (mV/A/m) × Ib × length / 1000, where mV/A/m is millivolts dropped per ampere of design current per metre, taken from the Appendix 4 cable tables.
The limits are 3% of the supply voltage for lighting and 5% for other circuits (6.9 V and 11.5 V on 230 V); the slides say to use a given supply voltage, so 5% of 395 V is 19.75 V.
The drop counts from the origin to the most distant point, so the submain's drop is added to the final circuit's; the formula sheet and project guide both say so.

When a three-phase submain feeds a single-phase final circuit, the formula sheet divides the submain's three-phase voltage drop by root 3 before adding it, and the project guide warns to calculate this correctly.
If the first cable fails, the slides increase the conductor CSA and repeat ("chasing the volt drop"); 1.5 mm² over 85 m fails, and 6.0 mm² gives 8.09 V.

The tabulated mV/A/m values are for the maximum conductor operating temperature, reached only at full load; at lower loads the cable is cooler and its resistance lower, which the factor Ct corrects (the Ct formula itself was not captured).
For cables above 16 mm² the tables give R, X and Z; the slides use Z where no power factor is known and R and X where one is.

The Ct formula, as printed in text by a reader on a cable-sizing page that attributes it to BS 7671 (Appendix 4 itself was not found in text): Ct = (230 + tp - (Ca² Cg² - Ib²/It²)(tp - 30)) / (230 + tp), with tp 70 °C for PVC and 90 °C for XLPE and It the tabulated current rating at 30 °C. TiSoft prints the same definitions of tp, Ib and It with the formula as a picture, and an IET EngX thread points to "the formula in 6.1 of Appendix 4" for it.

Why Ct exists: the tabulated mV/A/m are for the conductor at its maximum operating temperature, so a cable well below its rating runs cooler and drops less; TiSoft puts the saving at up to 20% for lightly loaded circuits, and the slides make the same point for the 6.0 mm² heater cable carrying 13.04 A of its 41 A.

Ct is worth applying only when Ib is well below It; with a heavy grouping factor and nothing else it comes to about 0.99 and is not worth the trouble (IET Electrical Installation Design Guide, quoted on EngX). The slides say it may let a smaller CSA than 6.0 mm² pass.

Contested or unsettled: which factors go into the Ct formula. The reader-quoted formula uses Ca and Cg (not Ci), and an EngX contributor says their design guide also counts only ambient temperature and grouping; the EngX thread asks why Ci is left out and gets the answer that Ci has already been used to choose It. The lesson uses Ca and Cg only and says so.

The slides' own heater example for the Ct step: 3 kW, 70 °C thermoplastic singles, Ca 0.94, 85 m, 29 mV/A/m in 1.5 mm² gives 32.14 V; 6.0 mm² (Iz 41 A in Table 4D1A, 7.3 mV/A/m in Table 4D1B) gives 8.09 V. Worked here (computed, not quoted): Ct for 6.0 mm² = (300 - (0.94² - 13.04²/41²) x 40) / 300 = 0.8957, so 8.09 V falls to 7.25 V; for 4.0 mm² (32 A in Table 4D1A, 11 mV/A/m in Table 4D1B) Ct = 0.9043, so 12.19 V tabulated falls to 11.03 V, under the 11.50 V limit.

The r, x and z columns appear only for cables over 16 mm² (the tables start them at 25 mm²); where the power factor is not known the z values are used, and where it is known the r and x values give a more accurate drop, because using z alone can give a drop higher than the actual one (Appendix 4 paragraph 6, as NICEIC reports it).

The power-factor expression, from a calculator site and from the impedance triangle Dan already has: drop per amp per metre = (mV/A/m)r x cos φ + (mV/A/m)x x sin φ, with sin φ = √(1 - cos² φ). NICEIC's worked 144 A, 0.75 lagging, 120 m motor in 70 mm² aluminium (r 0.90, x 0.14, z 0.92) comes to 16 V by z and 13.3 V by r and x, so the final circuit passes the 20 V limit once 5 V upstream is added.
Not found in text from any source: how Ct and the power factor combine (whether Ct multiplies only the r term). The lesson shows the two refinements separately and does not print a combined figure.

Table values from Dan's own copy, confirmed against the page images. Table 4E1B (90 °C thermosetting singles, voltage drop): in conduit, 2.5 mm² three-phase 16 mV/A/m; 1.5 mm² 27 three-phase and 31 for two cables single-phase; 25 mm² in conduit, three-phase, r 1.60, x 0.27, z 1.65. Table 4E1A (current-carrying capacity, Reference Method B, three or four cables): 1.5 mm² 20 A, 2.5 mm² 28 A.

A star-delta motor has six conductors from starter to motor, and in delta running its windings are three single-phase loads, so each conductor carries the winding current, line current ÷ √3. Turning that into a voltage drop is unsettled: one forum poster uses √3 x 58% of FLC x 2L x (R cos φ + X sin φ), another each conductor's impedance times its current. The course takes the first-principles reading (two conductors in series feed each winding: single-phase two-cable mV/A/m x winding current x length) and says it is its own reading, not BS 7671's.

The percentage limit for a three-phase circuit is taken of the three-phase voltage: 3% or 5% of 400 V is 12 V or 20 V, and a three-phase drop stays three-phase when the load is three-phase; only a three-phase submain feeding a single-phase final circuit is divided by √3.
Zs = Ze + (R1+R2): Ze is the external impedance of the supply and R1+R2 the circuit's own line and protective conductor resistance, which grows with length.
Calculated R1+R2 is (mΩ/m) × multiplier × length / 1000; the slides' 1.5 mm² line and cpc at 24.2 mΩ/m, multiplier 1.2 and 15 m gives 0.43 Ω, and Zs 0.64 Ω with Ze 0.21 Ω.
Loop impedance is limited because a lower Zs lets a higher fault current flow, which operates the device within the required time; the slides find 341.4 A at Cmin 0.95.
Cmin is the minimum voltage factor allowing for supply voltage variation, 0.95 for a low voltage supply under the ESQCR; the slides explain 230 V can fall to 218.5 V.
Final circuits to 32 A must disconnect in accordance with Table 41.1 (0.4 s in the slides' TN example), and these are maximum disconnection times, not actual ones.
Cmin is best used when deciding the fault current that operates a protective device, and Cmax and Cmin are not used together but in separate calculations.

The adiabatic check ensures the protective conductor can withstand the energy let-through of the device under earth fault conditions: S = √(I²t) / k, with k depending on conductor material, insulation and temperatures.
The slides take k from Tables 54.2 to 54.6 and, for the 1.5 mm² cpc, S = √(341.4² × 0.1) / 115 = 0.93 mm², and with Cmax at 395.3 A, 1.08 mm².
Cmax is advised when determining the fault current carrying capacity of conductors and Cmin for the current that operates the device.
The adiabatic equation is only valid for disconnection times not exceeding 5 seconds, and I²t is the energy let-through in A²s.
The live conductors must also withstand short circuit current: the slides find the minimum fault at Cmin (177.6 A), the maximum at Cmax (205.6 A), and t = k²S²/I² = 3.02 s for k = 143 and 2.5 mm².
IPF is whichever is highest of PEFC and PSCC, and the device's breaking capacity Icn must exceed it (IPF ≤ Icn) or the device may destroy itself in a short circuit or earth fault.
The project guide allows the SWA to be used as the cpc if justified by calculation, and flowchart note 2 separates a suitable cpc size from the minimum cpc size.
The assignment has five boards (MDB, DBL1, DBL2, DBP1, DBP2) and asks for a full design of the longest circuit from DBL2 and from DBP2, with relevant protective devices.

The project guide says to include all lengths of the cable run, calculations for thermal constraints, a comparison of Zs with the device's maximum, and the sum of all voltage drops from the intake equipment.
The formula sheet totals voltage drop as the submain's drop plus the final circuit's, and for a final circuit from a sub-board uses Zs = Zs@db + (R1+R2).
The showroom supply gives Ze 0.1 ohm, 4.6 kA prospective fault current and 20 degrees Celsius ambient; the motor and its cables are question 4.
Regulation 641.1 requires every installation, during erection and on completion, to be inspected and tested before being put into service.

Zs measured at ambient temperature must be allowed for the rise in conductor resistance under load before comparing with the maximum values; Megger describes an 80% rule, and a forum contributor says calculated R1+R2 should be for 70 degrees C.
To verify disconnection in 0.4 s on a TN system, the measured earth fault loop impedance must not exceed the corrected maximum, as the NICEIC example sets out for a 6 A type B breaker.

The Electrical Installation Certificate is valid only with the schedule of inspections and schedule(s) of test results, and the designer's recommended interval to the first periodic inspection must be entered.

The interval should reflect the frequency and quality of maintenance the installation can expect, agreed between designer, installer and others; for later reports Regulation 653.4 requires an explanation.
The assignment asks the designer to specify the maximum period to the first periodic inspection (9a) and to state the documents given to the client at handover (9b).
